The etymological and philosophical lineage from Greek *aletheia* through Roman *veritas* to modern *Wahrheit* is, for Heidegger, not a mere semantic history but a record of a progressive narrowing of the truth-event. *Aletheia*, in its pre-Socratic usage, is literally "un-concealment": the *a-* (not) negates *lethe* (forgetfulness, withdrawal), so that truth is the dynamic happening by which beings emerge from hiddenness into presence. It is an event, not a property. The Roman *veritas* (rooted in *ver-*, "to be true, to be faithful") gradually reconfigures this into a static correspondence between a propositional assertion and an object, a "correctness" that the modern *Wahrheit* inherits as a fixed attribute of well-formed statements. Heidegger's fundamental recovery is to insist that truth is, ontologically prior to any predication, an act of *Entbergen*—a bringing-into-the-open, a revealing. Within this ontology of disclosure, technology occupies not the marginal position of instrumental utility but the central ontological register: it is itself a *mode* of revealing. When Heidegger declares that "the essence of technology is a mode of revealing," he situates the technological alongside art, poetry, and metaphysics as a way in which the real is *hervorgebracht*—brought forth—into a particular kind of presence.

What distinguishes the technological revealing from earlier forms of disclosure is its operative structure, which Heidegger names *Herausfordern*, the "challenging-forth." A pre-modern craftsperson *lets* (wirken lässt) the material reveal itself within its own inner nature; the modern industrial apparatus, by contrast, *challenges* nature to arrange itself on demand, to yield quantifiable, interchangeable, storable energy. This is the logic of *Bestand*, standing-reserve: the river is no longer a river that reveals itself in its own rhythm but a "hydro-electric energy supplier"; the forest becomes "timber reserve"; the human being becomes "human resource." Yet this is undeniably a form of *aletheia*—something concealed is being drawn into the open, the hidden infrastructure of the real is being made visible and actionable. Technology reveals by *ordering*, and in ordering, it determines the very conditions under which something can appear as "real" in the modern epoch. The *Gestell* (enframing) is thus not a mechanism within a given world but the world's manner of self-disclosure.

Crucially, however, the aletheic structure is inherently dialectical: every *un*-concealing is simultaneously a new *concealment*. *A-letheia* contains its own *lethe*. The technological *Gestell*, in gathering (*versammeln*) all beings into the single mode of standing-reserve, conceals its own character as revealing and forecloses alternative disclosures—the contemplative, the poetic, the sacred. Heidegger's concept of *Geschick* (destining) names precisely this: we do not elect our mode of revealing but are *geschickt*, "sent," into it, and "the essence of all history is determined" by this gathering sending. The *Gefahr* (danger) is that the challenge-forth is mistaken for the only possible revealing, that the technological frame becomes the self-evident horizon of truth itself. Yet the *Rettung* (saving) resides in recognizing this as a destining rather than an essential identity: by *thinking* the essence of technology as one epochal form of *aletheia*, we become capable of *Gelassenheit*—a releasement into the manifold ways in which beings might otherwise disclose themselves. Technology, as a human way to reveal truth, is therefore neither a neutral tool nor an autonomous master; it is an epochal form of unconcealment within which both the deepest ontological danger and the possibility of a renewed, more primordial encounter with *aletheia* are, paradoxically, contained.

The crux of Wiles's second act in proving Fermat's Last Theorem lies in what is termed the "modular lifting problem": establishing that the modularity of the residual Galois representation ρ(E, p) for a single prime p > 3 necessarily implies the modularity of the full p-adic representation ρ(E, p^∞). This is not a merely technical extension but a foundational bridge in the proof architecture, because it permits the mathematician to verify modularity at the finite level ρ(E, p) and thereby inherit it for the infinite tower of representations ρ(E, p^n) as n ranges over all positive integers. Wiles's strategy was to approach this lifting through the machinery of Galois deformation theory, specifically by studying the universal deformation ring of the residual representation and showing that the associated Galois representation deforms modularly in a controlled fashion. The difficulty is substantial: one must demonstrate that the formal moduli space of such deformations is sufficiently rigid—typically by proving that the universal deformation ring is a complete intersection—so that the modularity property, once established at the special fiber, propagates upward through the entire family.

Within this deformation-theoretic framework, the proof bifurcates according to a critical structural property of the residual representation ρ(E, p): whether it is reducible or irreducible. A representation is reducible if its associated two-dimensional vector space admits a proper invariant subspace under the action of the absolute Galois group Q̄/Q; equivalently, the representation preserves a one-dimensional Galois-stable line. In the irreducible case, the absence of such a line means the representation acts irreducibly on C_p², and the deformation theory is governed by different cohomological and algebraic constraints. The irreducible path, which Wiles ultimately completed in his landmark 1995 paper, required a delicate interplay between the local deformation theory at p and the global Selmer group structure, with the key innovation being the construction of a "Taylor–Wiles" system of auxiliary primes to force the universal deformation ring to be a complete intersection.

The reducible case, while conceptually more constrained because the representation decomposes into characters, presents its own subtleties. Here the Galois representation splits as an extension of two one-dimensional characters, and the deformation must respect this extension structure. Wiles handled this scenario by exploiting the fact that reducibility imposes additional arithmetic information—namely, the existence of a rational p-isogeny on E—which can be leveraged to construct an auxiliary elliptic curve whose associated representation is irreducible. This reduction from the reducible to the irreducible setting allows the already-proved irreducible case to be invoked, closing the argument. The interplay between these two cases thus constitutes the architectural spine of the modularity lifting theorem, and its resolution was what finally permitted the contradiction to be derived from the hypothetical Frey curve, thereby establishing Fermat's Last Theorem in full generality.

# Borges' Library of Babel — Deterministic Page Generator

## Shell Script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# borges_library.sh
# Deterministic generator for any page of any book in Borges' Library of Babel.
#
# Library specification (per the problem statement):
#   • 25 characters : 22 lowercase letters (a–v), period, comma, space
#   • 410 pages     per book
#   • 40 lines      per page
#   • 80 characters per line
#   • 3 200 chars   per page  (40 × 80)
#   • 1 312 000     chars per book (410 × 3200)
#
# Usage:
#   ./borges_library.sh <book_index> <page_number>
#
#   book_index  – non-negative integer, 0-indexed (the "address" of the book)
#   page_number – integer from 1 to 410
#
# Example (deterministic — same inputs always yield the same page):
#   ./borges_library.sh 0 1
#   ./borges_library.sh 12345678901234567890 42
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail

# ─── argument handling ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [[ $# -lt 2 ]]; then
    cat >&2 <<EOF
Usage: $0 <book_index> <page_number>
  book_index   Non-negative integer (unique book address in the library)
  page_number  1 – 410
EOF
    exit 1
fi

BOOK_INDEX="$1"
PAGE_NUM="$2"

if ! [[ "$PAGE_NUM" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || (( PAGE_NUM < 1 || PAGE_NUM > 410 )); then
    echo "Error: page_number must be an integer between 1 and 410." >&2
    exit 1
fi

if ! [[ "$BOOK_INDEX" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    echo "Error: book_index must be a non-negative integer." >&2
    exit 1
fi

# ─── core generation (Python for arbitrary-precision arithmetic) ─────────────
python3 - "$BOOK_INDEX" "$PAGE_NUM" <<'PYEOF'
import sys

def generate_page(book_index: str, page_num: int) -> str:
    """
    Deterministically produce the 3 200 characters of page *page_num*
    of the book whose address is *book_index*.

    Mapping
    -------
    The book index N is interpreted as a base-25 integer whose digits
    (from least-significant to most-significant) are the characters of
    the book in reading order.  Page *p* (0-indexed) occupies digit
    positions [p·3200, (p+1)·3200).  We therefore compute

        page_value = N // 25^(p·3200)

    and then peel off 3 200 successive base-25 digits.
    """
    ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv., "   # 22 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 25
    BASE     = len(ALPHABET)                   # 25
    LINES    = 40
    COLS     = 80
    PAGE_LEN = LINES * COLS                    # 3 200

    n            = int(book_index)
    page_offset  = (page_num - 1) * PAGE_LEN   # 0-indexed start position

    # One big division to shift N so that the page's first char is the
    # least-significant base-25 digit.
    page_value   = n // (BASE ** page_offset)

    chars = []
    for _ in range(PAGE_LEN):
        chars.append(ALPHABET[page_value % BASE])
        page_value //= BASE

    flat  = "".join(chars)
    lines = [flat[i * COLS : (i + 1) * COLS] for i in range(LINES)]
    return "\n".join(lines)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bi = sys.argv[1]
    pn = int(sys.argv[2])
    print(generate_page(bi, pn))
PYEOF
```

## Academic Explanation: Combinatorial Structure and Indexing Logic

The Library of Babel, as formalised by the problem statement, is a finite (though astronomically vast) combinatorial object. The alphabet $\Sigma$ contains $|\Sigma| = 25$ symbols—twenty-two lowercase letters (a through v), the period, the comma, and the space character. Each book is a sequence of $n = 410 \times 40 \times 80 = 1{,}312{,}000$ characters drawn independently from $\Sigma$, so the total number of distinct books in the library is $|\Sigma|^n = 25^{1{,}312{,}000}$, a number with approximately $1.83 \times 10^6$ decimal digits. This is not an infinite set in the set-theoretic sense; rather, it is a finite but physically incomprehensible enumeration, and it is precisely this finiteness that makes a unique integer index for each book both meaningful and computable. The library's apparent infinity—debated by its fictional inhabitants—stems from the practical impossibility of traversing $25^{1.3\text{M}}$ hexagonal galleries, not from any mathematical unboundedness.

The indexing logic rests on the positional (base-$b$) numeral system generalised to an arbitrary alphabet. We assign each symbol in $\Sigma$ a digit value $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, 24\}$, and we interpret a book's full text as the base-25 expansion of its index $N$. Concretely, if the book's character at reading-order position $i$ (0-indexed from the first character of the first page) is $c_i$, then $d(c_i)$ is the $i$-th base-25 digit of $N$, i.e.\ $d(c_i) = \lfloor N / 25^i \rfloor \bmod 25$. To extract page $p$ (1-indexed, so $p \in \{1, \dots, 410\}$), we need digit positions $i = (p-1)\cdot 3200$ through $i = p\cdot 3200 - 1$. The script performs a single high-precision division $N' = \lfloor N / 25^{(p-1)\cdot 3200} \rfloor$, which shifts the window so that the page's first character becomes the least-significant digit of $N'$. It then peels off 3 200 successive digits via repeated modulo-and-divide by 25, mapping each digit back through the alphabet table. Because every arithmetic operation is on exact integers (Python's arbitrary-precision `int`), the mapping is a bijection: no two distinct indices can produce the same page, and every possible page of 3 200 characters from the 25-symbol alphabet appears exactly once across the $410$ pages of exactly one book.

The determinism of the construction follows directly from the uniqueness of base-$b$ representation. Given the pair $(N, p)$, the character at every one of the 3 200 positions is a pure function of these two integers; there is no random seed, no floating-point rounding, and no platform-dependent behaviour. This is the mathematical guarantee that a reader in any hexagonal chamber of the Library who knows the book's index and the page number will open the book to the same 40 lines of 80 characters as any other reader anywhere else in the universe. The script thus serves as a compact, executable proof of the principle: the Library contains *every* possible text, and a single integer together with a page number is sufficient to navigate it—no search, no stochastic sampling, merely arithmetic.

# Python Script: Nearest-Neighbor Textual Similarity in French Literary Corpus

```python
import numpy as np

# ─── Corpus ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
corpus = [
    "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
    "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
    "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
    "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
    "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
    "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
    "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
    "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
    "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
    "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,"
]

# ─── Character N-gram Extraction ───────────────────────────────────────────────
def char_ngrams(text: str, n: int = 3) -> list:
    """Extract all contiguous character n-grams from a lowercased string."""
    text = text.lower()
    return [text[i:i + n] for i in range(len(text) - n + 1)]

# ─── Vocabulary Construction ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
def build_vocabulary(ngrams_list: list) -> list:
    """Build a sorted, deduplicated vocabulary from all n-gram lists."""
    vocab = set()
    for ngrams in ngrams_list:
        vocab.update(ngrams)
    return sorted(vocab)

# ─── Vectorization ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def vectorize(text: str, vocab: list, n: int = 3) -> np.ndarray:
    """Map a text to a fixed-length frequency vector over the vocabulary."""
    ngrams = char_ngrams(text, n)
    vector = np.zeros(len(vocab))
    index_map = {ng: idx for idx, ng in enumerate(vocab)}
    for ng in ngrams:
        vector[index_map[ng]] += 1
    return vector

# ─── Cosine Similarity ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def cosine_similarity(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Compute the cosine of the angle between two vectors."""
    dot = np.dot(a, b)
    norm_a = np.linalg.norm(a)
    norm_b = np.linalg.norm(b)
    if norm_a == 0 or norm_b == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(dot / (norm_a * norm_b))

# ─── Main Pipeline ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
N_GRAM = 3
N = len(corpus)

# Step 1: Extract n-grams for every document
ngrams_list = [char_ngrams(text, N_GRAM) for text in corpus]

# Step 2: Build global vocabulary
vocab = build_vocabulary(ngrams_list)
print(f"Corpus size          : {N} strings")
print(f"Character 3-gram vocab: {len(vocab)} unique n-grams\n")

# Step 3: Vectorize
vectors = [vectorize(text, vocab, N_GRAM) for text in corpus]

# Step 4: Pairwise cosine similarity matrix
sim_matrix = np.zeros((N, N))
for i in range(N):
    for j in range(N):
        sim_matrix[i, j] = cosine_similarity(vectors[i], vectors[j])

# Step 5: Retrieve nearest neighbor (excluding self) for each text
print("=" * 80)
print(f"{'Nearest-Neighbor Results':^80}")
print("=" * 80)

for i in range(N):
    row = sim_matrix[i].copy()
    row[i] = -1.0  # mask self-similarity
    nearest_idx = int(np.argmax(row))
    sim_val = sim_matrix[i, nearest_idx]
    print(f"\n[{i}] \"{corpus[i]}\"")
    print(f"    → nearest: [{nearest_idx}] \"{corpus[nearest_idx]}\"")
    print(f"    → cosine similarity = {sim_val:.6f}")

print("\n" + "=" * 80)

# ─── Full similarity matrix (for inspection) ───────────────────────────────────
print("\nFull pairwise cosine-similarity matrix:")
header = "     " + "".join(f"{i:>7d}" for i in range(N))
print(header)
for i in range(N):
    row_str = f"{i:3d}  " + "".join(f"{sim_matrix[i][j]:7.4f}" for j in range(N))
    print(row_str)
```

## Academic Explanation: Vectorization, Distance Metrics, and Sparse String Comparison

**Paragraph 1 – Character N-Gram Vectorization.**
The script employs a character-level n-gram vectorization scheme (with *n* = 3, i.e., trigrams) to transform each French literary line into a high-dimensional numerical representation. Unlike word-level tokenization, character n-grams are particularly well suited to short, morphologically rich phrases in Romance languages, where inflectional endings (e.g., *‑eur*, *‑ée*, *‑ois*) and typographic artifacts (apostrophes, accents) carry substantial discriminative signal. Concretely, for a string of length *L* the function `char_ngrams` slides a window of width three across the lowercased text, yielding *L* − 2 substrings.     dx = SIGMA * (y - x)
    dy = x * (RHO - z) - y
    dz = x * y - BETA * z
    return np.array([dx, dy, dz])

# 2. Classic RK4 integrator
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
def rk4_step(f, state: np.ndarray, dt: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Single 4th-order Runge-Kutta step."""
    k1 = f(state)
    k2 = f(state + 0.5 * dt * k1)
    k3 = f(state + 0.5 * dt * k2)
    k4 = f(state + dt * k3)
    return state + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)


def integrate_rk4(f, x0: np.ndarray, t_end: float, dt: float):
    """
    Integrate ODE y' = f(y) from t=0 to t_end using fixed-step RK4.
    Returns (time array, state array of shape (N, 3)).
    """
    n_steps = int(np.round(t_end / dt))
    t = np.linspace(0.0, t_end, n_steps + 1)
    states = np.empty((n_steps + 1, 3))
    states[0] = x0
    for i in range(n_steps):
        states[i + 1] = rk4_step(f, states[i], dt)
    return t, states

def lorenz(state: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:

    x, y, z = state

    dy = x * (RHO - z) - y

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Molecular Graph Topology, ECFP4 Fingerprinting, and Pairwise Tanimoto Similarity
=================================================================================
Compares Aspirin, Caffeine, and Ibuprofen via:
  1. Topological adjacency matrices (NetworkX)
  2. Circular (Morgan) ECFP4 fingerprints (RDKit)
  3. Pairwise Tanimoto (Jaccard) similarity matrix

Requirements:
    pip install rdkit numpy networkx pandas
"""

import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
import pandas as pd
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem, DataStructs
from rdkit import RDLogger

# Suppress RDKit's informational chatter for clean output
RDLogger.DisableLog('rdApp.*')

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. Define the three molecules (simplified SMILES)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
molecules = {
    "Aspirin":    "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O",
    "Caffeine":   "CN1C=NC2=C1C(=O)N(C(=O)N2C)C",
    "Ibuprofen":  "CC(C)Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C)C(=O)O",
}

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2. Helper: build a NetworkX graph + adjacency matrix from an RDKit Mol
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
def build_graph_and_adjacency(mol: Chem.Mol) -> tuple[nx.Graph, np.ndarray, dict[int, str]]:
    """
    Convert an RDKit molecule into an undirected NetworkX graph and
    return the (N×N) adjacency matrix together with an atom-label map.
    """
    G = nx.Graph()
    atom_labels = {}

    # Add nodes (atoms) – skip dummy / explicit-H placeholders
    for atom in mol.GetAtoms():
        idx = atom.GetIdx()
        if atom.GetSymbol() == "":
            continue
        G.add_node(idx, label=atom.GetSymbol())
        atom_labels[idx] = atom.GetSymbol()

    # Add edges (bonds) – one undirected edge per bond
    for bond in mol.GetBonds():
        a1 = bond.GetBeginAtomIdx()
        a2 = bond.GetEndAtomIdx()
        # Only add if both atoms were kept
        if a1 in G.nodes and a2 in G.nodes:
            G.add_edge(a1, a2, order=int(bond.GetBondTypeAsDouble()))

    # Re-index nodes to 0..N-1 for a clean matrix
    mapping = {old: new for new, old in enumerate(G.nodes())}
    G = nx.relabel_nodes(G, mapping)

    adj_matrix = nx.to_numpy_array(G, dtype=int)  # N×N binary matrix
    return G, adj_matrix, {mapping[k]: v for k, v in atom_labels.items()}


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 3. Compute ECFP4 (Morgan, radius = 2) fingerprints
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
def ecfp4_fingerprint(mol: Chem.Mol, n_bits: int = 2048) -> DataStructs.ExpBitVec:
    """
    ECFP4 == circular fingerprint with a radius of 2 (diameter 4).
    RDKit's GetMorganFingerprintAsBitVec(radius=2) is the standard
    implementation.  The 2048-bit fixed-length vector is the de facto
    standard in cheminformatics pipelines.
    """
    return AllChem.GetMorganFingerprintAsBitVec(mol, radius=2, nBits=n_bits)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 4. Tanimoto (Jaccard) similarity on two bit vectors
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
def tanimoto(fp1: DataStructs.ExpBitVec, fp2: DataStructs.ExpBitVec) -> float:
    """
    Tanimoto  T(A,B)  =  |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|
    For sparse bit-vectors this equals  (A·B) / (|A| + |B| - A·B).
    """
    return DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fp1, fp2)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 5. Main pipeline
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
def main():
    names = list(molecules.keys())
    mols: dict[str, Chem.Mol] = {}
    fps: dict[str, DataStructs.ExpBitVec] = {}
    adjacency_data: dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}
    graph_objects: dict[str, nx.Graph] = {}

    print("=" * 72)
    print("  MOLECULAR GRAPH TOPOLOGY  ·  ECFP4  ·  TANIMOTO SIMILARITY")
    print("=" * 72)

    # --- Parse & build graphs ------------------------------------------
    for name, smi in molecules.items():
        mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
        if mol is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Failed to parse SMILES for {name}: {smi}")
        mol = Chem.AddHs(mol)          # explicit H's (optional; we'll strip)
        mol = Chem.RemoveHs(mol)      # work with heavy-atom skeleton

        G, adj, labels = build_graph_and_adjacency(mol)
        mols[name] = mol
        graph_objects[name] = G
        adjacency_data[name] = adj

        n_atoms = adj.shape[0]
        n_bonds = G.number_of_edges()
        print(f"\n┌─ {name}")
        print(f"│  SMILES        : {smi}")
        print(f"│  Heavy atoms   : {n_atoms}")
        print(f"│  Bonds         : {n_bonds}")
        print(f"│  Atom labels   : {sorted(set(labels.values()))}")
        print(f"│  Adjacency matrix ({n_atoms}×{n_atoms}):")
        print("│" + " " * 6 + str(np.array2string(adj, separator=",").replace("\n", "\n" + "│" + " " * 6)))
        print("└─" + "─" * 56)

    # --- ECFP4 fingerprints -------------------------------------------
    for name, mol in mols.items():
        fp = ecfp4_fingerprint(mol, n_bits=2048)
        fps[name] = fp
        n_bits_set = sum(1 for b in fp if b)
        print(f"  {name:<12s}  ECFP4 (2048-bit):  {n_bits_set:>3d} bits set  "
              f"  ({100*n_bits_set/2048:.1f}% density)")

    # --- Pairwise Tanimoto matrix --------------------------------------
    print(f"\n{'─' * 72}")
    print("  PAIRWISE TANIMOTO (JACCARD) SIMILARITY MATRIX")
    print(f"{'─' * 72}")

    sim_matrix = np.zeros((len(names), len(names)))
    for i, ni in enumerate(names):
        for j, nj in enumerate(names):
            sim_matrix[i, j] = tanimoto(fps[ni], fps[nj])

    # Pretty-print as a DataFrame
    df = pd.DataFrame(sim_matrix, index=names, columns=names)
    print("\n" + df.to_string(float_format=lambda x: f"{x:.4f}"))

    # Also print as a plain-text triangle
    print("\n  Triangular view (i ≤ j):")
    for i in range(len(names)):
        for j in range(i, len(names)):
            if i == j:
                print(f"    T({names[i]}, {names[j]}) = {sim_matrix[i, j]:.4f}   (self)")
            else:
                print(f"    T({names[i]}, {names[j]}) = {sim_matrix[i, j]:.4f}")

    # --- Bonus: Tanimoto *distance* (1 − T) ----------------------------

"""
Comparative Benchmark: Naive Array vs. Segment Tree
for Point Updates and Range Sum Queries.

N = 100,000 elements | Q = 50,000 mixed operations (updates + queries)
"""

import time
import random
import sys

# Increase recursion limit for safety (tree height is ~17, but build is depth-first)
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. NAIVE CONTINUOUS ARRAY STRATEGY
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

def naive_build(arr: list) -> list:
    """Return a working copy of the input array."""
    return arr[:]


def naive_point_update(arr: list, index: int, value: int) -> None:
    """O(1) point update: overwrite a single element."""
    arr[index] = value


def naive_range_sum(arr: list, l: int, r: int) -> int:
    """O(k) range sum where k = r - l + 1. Worst case O(N)."""
    total = 0
    for i in range(l, r + 1):
        total += arr[i]
    return total


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2. SEGMENT TREE (iterative-free, recursive)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

class SegmentTree:
    """
    Classic recursive segment tree stored in a 4N-sized flat array.
    Supports:
      - Build        : Θ(N)
      - Point Update : Θ(log N)
      - Range Query  : Θ(log N)
    """

    def __init__(self, arr: list):
        self.n = len(arr)
        self.tree = [0] * (4 * self.n)   # standard 4N allocation
        self._build(1, 0, self.n - 1, arr)

    # ── internal helpers ──────────────────
    def _build(self, node: int, start: int, end: int, arr: list) -> None:
        if start == end:
            self.tree[node] = arr[start]
            return
        mid = (start + end) >> 1
        self._build(2 * node,     start,     mid, arr)
        self._build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1,   end, arr)
        self.tree[node] = self.tree[2 * node] + self.tree[2 * node + 1]

    def _update(self, node: int, start: int, end: int,
                idx: int, val: int) -> None:
        if start == end:
            self.tree[node] = val
            return
        mid = (start + end) >> 1
        if idx <= mid:
            self._update(2 * node,     start, mid,     idx, val)
        else:
            self._update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, end,   idx, val)
        self.tree[node] = self.tree[2 * node] + self.tree[2 * node + 1]

    def _query(self, node: int, start: int, end: int,
               l: int, r: int) -> int:
        if r < start or end < l:          # no overlap
            return 0
        if l <= start and end <= r:       # full overlap
            return self.tree[node]
        mid = (start + end) >> 1          # partial overlap → recurse both
        return (self._query(2 * node,     start, mid,   l, r)
              + self._query(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, end, l, r))

    # ── public API ────────────────────────
    def point_update(self, idx: int, val: int) -> None:
        self._update(1, 0, self.n - 1, idx, val)

    def range_sum(self, l: int, r: int) -> int:
        return self._query(1, 0, self.n - 1, l, r)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 3. SYNTHETIC WORKLOAD GENERATOR
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

def generate_workload(n: int, q: int, rng: random.Random) -> list:
    """
    Produce a list of Q operations.
    Each op is a tuple:
      ('update', index, value)
      ('query',  l,     r)
    50 % updates, 50 % queries.
    """
    ops = []
    for _ in range(q):
        if rng.random() < 0.5:
            idx = rng.randrange(n)
            val = rng.randrange(1, 1001)
            ops.append(('update', idx, val))
        else:
            l = rng.randrange(n)
            r = rng.randrange(l, n)
            ops.append(('query', l, r))
    return ops


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 4. BENCHMARK HARNESS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

def benchmark_naive(arr_orig: list, ops: list) -> float:
    arr = naive_build(arr_orig)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == 'update':
            naive_point_update(arr, op[1], op[2])
        else:
            naive_range_sum(arr, op[1], op[2])
    return time.perf_counter() - t0


def benchmark_segment_tree(arr_orig: list, ops: list) -> float:
    st = SegmentTree(arr_orig)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == 'update':
            st.point_update(op[1], op[2])
        else:
            st.range_sum(op[1], op[2])
    return time.perf_counter() - t0


def main():
    N = 100_000
    Q = 50_000
    SEED = 42

    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    arr = [rng.randrange(1, 1001) for _ in range(N)]
    ops = generate_workload(N, Q, rng)

    print("=" * 62)
    print(f"  N = {N:,} elements   |   Q = {Q:,} mixed operations")
    print(f"  (≈50 % point updates, ≈50 % range-sum queries)")
    print("=" * 62)

    # ── Naive ─────────────────────────────
    t_naive = benchmark_naive(arr, ops)
    print(f"\n  [Naive Array]   total wall-clock : {t_naive:>10.4f} s")

    # ── Segment Tree ──────────────────────
    t_seg = benchmark_segment_tree(arr, ops)
    print(f"  [Segment Tree]  total wall-clock : {t_seg:>10.4f} s")

    # ── Speedup ───────────────────────────
    speedup = t_naive / t_seg if t_seg > 0 else float('inf')
    print(f"\n  Speedup (Naive / SegTree)        : {speedup:>10.1f}×")
    print("=" * 62)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Let *N* denote the array length and *Q* the number of intermixed operations. For the **naive contiguous array**, a point update executes in Θ(1) time (a single indexed write), while a range-sum query over an interval of length *k = r − l + 1* requires Θ(*k*) arithmetic operations, giving a worst-case bound of O(*N*) and a lower bound of Ω(1) (a single-element query). """
Computational Musicology & DSP: C-Major Triad Synthesis with Harmonic Overtone Injection
=========================================================================================
Synthesizes a 1-second C-Major triad (C4, E4, G4) with logarithmically decaying
2nd and 3rd harmonic overtones, then extracts and identifies spectral peaks via FFT.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import rfft, rfftfreq
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
import warnings

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. SIGNAL SYNTHESIS PARAMETERS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
SAMPLE_RATE = 44100          # Hz
DURATION    = 1.0            # seconds
N_SAMPLES   = int(SAMPLE_RATE * DURATION)

# C-Major Triad fundamental frequencies (Hz)
FUNDAMENTALS = {
    "C4": 261.63,
    "E4": 329.63,
    "G4": 392.00,
}

# Harmonics to inject: 1st (fundamental), 2nd, 3rd
HARMONICS = [1, 2, 3]

def log_decay_amplitude(n: int) -> float:
    """
    Compute the amplitude for the n-th harmonic using a natural
    logarithmic decay: A(n) = 1 / (1 + ln(n)).
    
    This models the perceptual and physical roll-off of higher
    partials in most acoustic instruments.
    """
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.log(n))

def synthesize_triad() -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Construct the time-domain waveform of the C-Major triad with
    2nd and 3rd harmonic overtones at logarithmically decaying amplitudes.
    """
    # Time axis: t = [0, 1/Ns, 2/Ns, ..., (Ns-1)/Ns]
    t = np.arange(N_SAMPLES) / SAMPLE_RATE

    signal = np.zeros(N_SAMPLES, dtype=np.float64)

    for note_name, f0 in FUNDAMENTALS.items():
        note_signal = np.zeros(N_SAMPLES, dtype=np.float64)
        for n in HARMONICS:
            amp  = log_decay_amplitude(n)
            freq = n * f0
            # Add a phase of zero for all components (coherent onset)
            note_signal += amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * freq * t)
        signal += note_signal

    # Normalize to avoid clipping (peak amplitude ~1.0)
    peak = np.max(np.abs(signal))
    if peak > 0:
        signal = signal / peak

    return signal

def extract_spectral_peaks(signal: np.ndarray) -> None:
    """
    Apply the Real FFT, identify frequency peaks, and print a
    structured report of detected spectral components.
    """
    # Real FFT (signal is real-valued → exploit conjugate symmetry)
    spectrum = rfft(signal)
    magnitude = np.abs(spectrum)

    # Frequency bins corresponding to each FFT bin
    freqs = rfftfreq(N_SAMPLES, d=1.0 / SAMPLE_RATE)

    # Peak detection: use a threshold relative to the maximum magnitude
    # and a minimum distance to separate closely-spaced harmonics
    peak_height_threshold = 0.05 * np.max(magnitude)   # 5 % of max
    peak_distance = int(0.02 * len(freqs))             # ~2 % of bins minimum separation

    peak_indices, peak_properties = find_peaks(
        magnitude,
        height=peak_height_threshold,
        distance=peak_distance,
        prominence=0.03 * np.max(magnitude),
    )

    peak_frequencies = freqs[peak_indices]
    peak_magnitudes  = magnitude[peak_indices]

    # ── Print structured report ──
    print("=" * 72)
    print("  SPECTRAL PEAK ANALYSIS — C-MAJOR TRIAD WITH HARMONIC OVERTONES")
    print(f"  Sample Rate: {SAMPLE_RATE} Hz | Duration: {DURATION} s | "
          f"Samples: {N_SAMPLES:,}")
    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"  {'Peak #':<8}{'Frequency (Hz)':<18}{'Magnitude':<14}"
          f"{'Expected Source'}")
    print("  " + "-" * 68)

    # Build a lookup of all expected frequencies for annotation
    expected_freqs = []
    for note_name, f0 in FUNDAMENTALS.items():
        for n in HARMONICS:
            expected_freqs.append((n * f0, f"{note_name} H{n}"))

    for i, (freq, mag) in enumerate(zip(peak_frequencies, peak_magnitudes), 1):
        # Find the closest expected frequency within ±2 Hz
        closest = None
        closest_diff = np.inf
        for ef, label in expected_freqs:
            diff = abs(freq - ef)
            if diff < closest_diff:
                closest_diff = diff
                closest = label
        annotation = closest if closest_diff < 2.0 else "—"
        print(f"  {i:<8}{freq:<18.2f}{mag:<14.4f}{annotation}")

    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"  Total peaks detected: {len(peak_frequencies)}")
    print(f"  Frequency resolution: {SAMPLE_RATE / N_SAMPLES:.4f} Hz/bin")
    print("=" * 72)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2. EXECUTION
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("\n[1] Synthesizing C-Major triad waveform ...")
    waveform = synthesize_triad()
    print(f"    Waveform shape: {waveform.shape}, dtype: {waveform.dtype}")
    print(f"    Peak amplitude: {np.max(np.abs(waveform)):.6f}")
    print(f"    RMS:            {np.sqrt(np.mean(waveform**2)):.6f}")
    print()

    print("[2] Computing FFT and extracting spectral peaks ...")
    extract_spectral_peaks(waveform)
    print()

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) constitutes the foundational bridge between the time domain and the frequency domain in digital signal processing. For a discrete sequence $x[n]$ of length $N$, the DFT is defined as the complex-valued sum:

Fetal testosterone must cross the blood–brain barrier, where tissue-specific aromatase (CYP19A1) converts a fraction of it to estradiol, which then engages ERα and ERβ receptors on neural progenitors, interneurons, and glial cells. Structures such as the caudal bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3) show group-level sex differences in volume or neuron number, yet these differences are modest, overlap heavily across sexes, and are mediated by interacting pathways—glucocorticoid-receptor signaling, interleukin-1β–driven neuroinflammation, neurotrophic factors (BDNF, NGF), and the relative ratio of estrogen to androgen receptor expression—rather than by a single deterministic gene or hormone.

At the molecular level, the relevant genetic loci (e.g., ESR1, AR, CYP19A1) are expressed in a tissue- and time-specific mosaic; epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation at the ESR1 promoter, histone acetylation states) set the sensitivity of each neuronal subpopulation to circulating steroids. Prenatal environmental variables—maternal glucocorticoid exposure, immune activation (elevated IL-6, TNF-α), psychosocial stress, and subtle variations in fetal testosterone production—can shift the probability distribution of cell fates without producing a qualitatively different organ. In other words, the BSTc or INAH3 does not "decide" a sex at a single moment; rather, a continuum of neuroendocrine, epigenetic, and stochastic inputs nudges developmental trajectories within a range, and the resulting adult morphology is an emergent, partially heritable but environmentally modulated outcome. This is a fundamentally different developmental logic from the binary, paracrine logic of ductal differentiation, and it is why the brain exhibits sex differences that are statistical tendencies rather than invariant switches.

Whether these prenatal neuroendocrine imprints constitute a "hardwiring" of gender identity is a claim the evidence does not support in the strong, deterministic sense the phrase implies. First, the identified structures (INAH3, BSTc, the hypothalamic GnRH system, the preoptic area) are involved in hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis regulation, stress reactivity, and social behavior; no study has demonstrated that they are necessary or sufficient for the subjective experience of gender identity, which is a higher-order, reflective self-concept implicating prefrontal, limbic, and default-mode networks that are themselves highly plastic. Second, the magnitude of group-level sex differences in these nuclei is small relative to within-group variance, and many of the studies rest on small, convenience samples of cadaveric or imaging data with uncontrolled confounds (hormone therapy, surgical status, diagnostic labeling). Third, even under the classical organizational–activational framework (Phoenix, Goy & Gerall, 1959), prenatal programming sets a *bias* or *range of likely trajectories*, not a fixed point; postnatal experience, social feedback, language, and ongoing epigenetic remodeling continue to reshape circuitry well into adulthood. Finally, the conceptual leap from "there are prenatal sex differences in hypothalamic nuclei" to "gender identity is determined before birth" conflates a low-level neuroendocrine bias with a complex, multi-system, socially mediated identity, committing what might be called a category error between proximate biology and distal selfhood. A more defensible position is that prenatal neuroendocrine and genetic factors contribute one layer among many—genetic (including but not limited to sex-chromosome gene expression), endocrine, epigenetic, social, and psychological—to the enormously variable phenomenology of gender, and that no single "switch" in the fetal brain dictates who a person will be.

The Greek *aletheia* and the Latin *veritas* are, in Heidegger's reading, not synonymous with the post-Kantian correspondence theory of truth whereby a judgment matches a pre-given object. *A-letheia* is the prefix *a-* (not, un-) joined to *lêthê* (forgetting, concealment): truth is, in its most primordial sense, the event in which what had been concealed is permitted to emerge into the open (*das Offene*). *Veritas* inherits from the root *vēr-* (to be true, to be what is) a similar orientation toward the happening of presence rather than toward a static property of propositions. Heidegger's term *Entbergen* (unconcealing) crystallizes this inheritance: truth is not something a subject asserts but an ontological event in which *dasein* is drawn into a disclosure and something "comes into the open." Crucially, this means that every epochal mode of "bringing-forth" (*Hervorbringen*)—whether artistic, contemplative, or technological—is, in a broad and fundamental sense, a mode of *aletheia*, a way in which the real (*das Reale*) is let be and thereby disclosed. To ask how technology reveals truth is therefore not to reduce truth to a human epistemic achievement but to trace one particular epochal sending (*Schicken*) of disclosure.

Heidegger insists that the essence of technology is "nothing technological" in the instrumental sense; its essence lies in its role as a *mode of revealing*. In *Anaximander* and the Homeric *poiesis*, in theic showing-forth and in human bringing-forth, the Greeks already discerned four ways in which *aletheia* happens. Modern technology, understood as *Gestell* (Enframing), constitutes a fifth and uniquely totalizing mode: it "challenges forth" (*herausfordert*) nature to yield up energy, organizing every entity—river, landscape, the human being included—as *Bestand* (standing-reserve). Yet this ordering is not the negation of disclosure; it is a specific, radical happening of *Entbergen*. The real is disclosed, but it is disclosed *as* resource, *as* something calculable and dispatchable. In this sense technology is a truth-happening: it gathers the world into a coherent, intelligible field of reference, and it is precisely this gathering that Heidegger calls the "sending that gathers" (*versammelde Schicken*). Technology does not stand outside truth; it is an epochal form of *aletheia* in which the open is structured around availability and interchangeability.

The deeper ground of this sending is what Heidegger names *Geschick* (destining), and it is from this destining that the essence of all *Geschichte* (history) is determined. History, properly understood, is neither the chronicle of human deeds nor the mere sequence of events; it is the unfolding of the way Being sends its own disclosure in a given epoch. The particular destining of modernity—the destining into "objectifying representation"—is what renders the historical accessible as an object for the sciences and, consequently, what licenses the conflation of the historical with the merely chronicled. The danger (*Gefahr*) of this destining is that it forecloses other modes of *aletheia*: the poetic, the contemplative, the devotional are absorbed into the regime of the calculable. Yet Heidegger locates the saving power (*Rettung*) precisely within the same destining, because only the one who has encountered the essence of the sending from within can achieve a "grateful release" (*dankbare Freisein*) from its dominion. Technology, as an epochal way of truth, is thus simultaneously the most radical disclosure and the most perilous concealment: it reveals the world in its totality as *Bestand* while concealing the very ground of disclosure that makes any revealing possible.

The modular lifting problem constitutes the technical core of Wiles's proof and demands a transition from the finite-level representation ρ(E, p) to the full p-adic representation ρ(E, p^∞). Concretely, one is given a residual Galois representation \bar{ρ}: G_Q → GL₂(ℤ/pℤ) associated to the elliptic curve E and must demonstrate the existence of a compatible system of representations over ℤ_p that specializes to \bar{ρ} and is itself modular. Wiles recasts this existence question within the framework of Galois deformation theory, following the foundational work of Mazur. One introduces the universal deformation ring R over ℤ_p, which parametrizes all lifts of \bar{ρ} satisfying prescribed local conditions at primes of bad reduction and at infinity, and one then must show that the natural surjection from the corresponding Hecke algebra T (governing modular forms of appropriate weight and level) onto R is in fact an isomorphism. The difficulty is that R is a highly nontrivial, potentially non-reduced ring whose structure is not immediately accessible; one must control both its tangent space (the space of infinitesimal deformations) and its global algebraic structure simultaneously.

A critical branching in the argument arises from the dichotomy between reducible and irreducible residual representations. In the irreducible case, the deformation theory is well-behaved: the universal deformation ring R is (under suitable hypotheses) a regular local ring of dimension one, and the tangent space computation reduces to comparing dimensions via Euler characteristic formulas on the associated cohomology groups. The Hecke algebra T, being Gorenstein and of the same dimension, then maps onto R with finite kernel, and a standard Nakayama-type argument together with a comparison of Hilbert-Samuel multiplicities yields the desired isomorphism. In the reducible case, by contrast, the deformation functor acquires a substantially more complicated structure; the universal deformation ring can have embedded components or fail to be regular, and the naive dimension-counting argument breaks down because the space of pseudomorphisms and the space of true morphisms may diverge. This forced Wiles to develop the "Taylor-Wiles patches," a level-lifting argument that temporarily replaces the representation at level N with one at a larger level Nq (where q is a carefully chosen auxiliary prime), in the enlarged setting the deformation ring regains regularity, the isomorphism can be established, and the result is then descended back to the original level.

The resolution of the reducible case ultimately required the key estimate comparing the order of the Selmer group at the original level with the order of the corresponding group at the patched level, a computation involving the arithmetic of Hecke operators and the action of the Galois group on the cohomology of the modular curve. Wiles's original 1995 paper contained a gap in precisely this reducible case, which was subsequently repaired by a joint argument with Taylor in 1996. The full proof thus rests on the interplay of commutative algebra (the structure of R and T), Galois cohomology (the control of H¹ and H² groups), and the arithmetic of modular forms (the Hecke eigenvalues and their specialization), all organized within the deformation-theoretic framework that reduces the global modularity question to a local algebraic statement about a single universal ring.

## Academic Explanation: Combinatorics and Indexing Logic

**Paragraph 1 — The combinatorial space and the bijection with ℕ.** Borges conceives each book as a fixed-length string of 524 800 characters (410 pages × 40 lines × 32 characters per line), drawn from an alphabet of 25 symbols (the twenty-two letters *a* through *v*, the space, the period, and the comma). The set of all such books therefore has cardinality 25^{524 800}, an integer with roughly 733 710 decimal digits. Crucially, this cardinality is a *countable* infinity only in the meta-sense; the library is a finite (if incomprehensibly vast) set. By the fundamental theorem of bijections between finite sets of equal size, the set {0, 1, 2, …, 25^{524 800} − 1} is in one-to-one correspondence with the set of all books. The script exploits this by treating the integer *N* (the "book index") as a number expressed in base 25: writing *N* in base 25 yields a 524 800-digit string (zero-padded on the left if *N* has fewer digits), and the *i*-th digit *c_i* satisfies *c_i* = ⌊*N* / 25^*i*⌋ mod 25. Mapping each *c_i* through the ordered 25-symbol alphabet produces the *i*-th character of the book, establishing a deterministic, invertible encoding.

**Paragraph 2 — Page-level extraction via successive quotient-remainder division.** A reader requests page *P* (1 ≤ *P* ≤ 410). The global character positions spanned by that page are *s* = (*P* − 1) × 1 280 through *s* + 1 279. Rather than computing 25^{*s*} for each individual character (which would require 1 280 separate large-integer exponentiations), the script performs a single "shift": *M* = ⌊*N* / 25^{*s*}⌋. This right-shifts the base-25 representation by *s* positions, so that *M*'s least-significant base-25 digit is exactly *c_s*, the first character of the requested page. The script then peels off digits sequentially: for *j* = 0, 1, …, 1 279 it computes *d_j* = *M* mod 25 and sets *M* ← ⌊*M* / 25⌋. Each iteration is a single division of a (shrinking) big integer by the small constant 25, an O(1) operation on the number of machine words involved per step. After 1 280 iterations the page is fully materialised. The total work is dominated by the initial shift (one big-integer division whose operands may each have hundreds of thousands of digits), which modern arbitrary-precision libraries (CPython's `_PyLong` internals, based on Knuth's Algorithm D) execute in O(*n*²) time in the number of base-2^{30} limbs *n*—well within a second even for the maximum page number.

**Paragraph 3 — Determinism, injectivity, and philosophical correspondence.** Because the mapping *N* ↦ (base-25 expansion) is a bijection and the page-extraction procedure is a pure function of *N* and *P*, the script is fully deterministic: the same pair of arguments always yields the identical 40-line page, with no randomness, no filesystem state, and no network dependency. Two distinct indices *N₁* ≠ *N₂* differ in at least one base-25 digit position *i*; if *i* falls within the span of page *P*, the generated pages differ in that character, preserving the injectivity of the original bijection at the page level. This mirrors Borges' ontological claim that the Library contains *every* possible text—every theorem, every poem, every corrupted fragment of every other book—and that the "reader" need only know the correct index. The script does not search the Library; it *decodes* a single address into its characters, transforming an act of cosmic enumeration into a finite, reproducible arithmetic operation. The combinatorial explosion (25^{524 800}) is never materialised; only a 1 280-digit window into it is extracted, demonstrating how positional notation compresses an infinite-seeming space into a single integer and a single modulus loop.

import numpy as np
from collections import Counter


def get_char_ngrams(text, n=3):
    """Extract character n-grams from a string (lowercased)."""
    text = text.lower().replace("œ", "oe")  # normalize ligatures
    ngrams = []
    for i in range(len(text) - n + 1):
        ngrams.append(text[i:i + n])
    return ngrams


def build_vocabulary(corpus, n=3):
    """Construct the global vocabulary of all character n-grams."""
    vocab = set()
    for text in corpus:
        vocab.update(get_char_ngrams(text, n))
    return sorted(vocab)


def vectorize(text, vocab_index, n=3):
    """Represent a text as a sparse count vector over the n-gram vocabulary."""
    vec = np.zeros(len(vocab_index), dtype=np.float64)
    for ng in get_char_ngrams(text, n):
        if ng in vocab_index:
            vec[vocab_index[ng]] += 1.0
    return vec


def cosine_similarity_matrix(vectors):
    """Compute the full pairwise cosine similarity matrix."""
    norms = np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    norms[norms == 0] = 1e-10  # guard against zero vectors
    normalized = vectors / norms
    return normalized @ normalized.T


def find_nearest_neighbors(corpus, ngram_size=3):
    """
    For each text i, find the text j (j ≠ i) that maximizes
    cosine similarity cos(i, j) = (v_i · v_j) / (||v_i|| · ||v_j||).
    """
    # --- Vectorization phase ---
    vocabulary = build_vocabulary(corpus, n=ngram_size)
    vocab_index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vocabulary)}
    vectors = np.array([vectorize(text, vocab_index, n=ngram_size) for text in corpus])

    # --- Similarity phase ---
    sim_matrix = cosine_similarity_matrix(vectors)

    # --- Nearest-neighbor extraction (exclude self) ---
    results = []
    for i in range(len(corpus)):
        row = sim_matrix[i].copy()
        row[i] = -np.inf  # mask self-similarity
        nearest_idx = int(np.argmax(row))
        results.append({
            "index": i,
            "text": corpus[i],
            "nearest_index": nearest_idx,
            "nearest_text": corpus[nearest_idx],
            "cosine_similarity": float(sim_matrix[i, nearest_idx]),
        })

    return results, sim_matrix

    k3 = func(state + 0.5 * dt * k2, *args)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def lorenz(state: np.ndarray, sigma: float, beta: float, rho: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Return the right-hand side of the Lorenz equations.

    dx/dt = sigma * (y - x)
    dy/dt = x * (rho - z) - y
    dz/dt = x * y - beta * z
    """
    x, y, z = state
    dxdt = sigma * (y - x)
    dydt = x * (rho - z) - y
    dzdt = x * y - beta * z
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt, dzdt])

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Explicit 4th-Order Runge-Kutta (RK4) Integrator
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def rk4_integrate(initial_state: np.ndarray,
                  dt: float,
                  n_steps: int,
                  sigma: float,
                  beta: float,
                  rho: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Integrate the Lorenz system using classical RK4.

    Parameters
    ----------
    initial_state : (3,) array – [x0, y0, z0]
    dt            : time-step size
    n_steps       : number of integration steps
    sigma, beta, rho : Lorenz parameters

    Returns
    -------
    trajectory : (n_steps+1, 3) array of states
    """
    trajectory = np.empty((n_steps + 1, 3))
    trajectory[0] = initial_state

    for i in range(n_steps):
        s = initial_state
        k1 = lorenz(s, sigma, beta, rho)
        k2 = lorenz(s + 0.5 * dt * k1, sigma, beta, rho)
        k3 = lorenz(s + 0.5 * dt * k2, sigma, beta, rho)
        k4 = lorenz(s + dt * k3, sigma, beta, rho)

        initial_state = s + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0*k2 + 2.0*k3 + k4)
        trajectory[i + 1] = initial_state

    return trajectory

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Comparative Benchmark: Naive Array vs. Segment Tree
for Dynamic Range Sum Queries with Point Updates.

N = 100,000 elements | Q = 50,000 intermixed operations
"""

import time
import random
import sys

# Increase recursion limit to safely handle segment tree construction
sys.setrecursionlimit(500_000)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
#  1. NAIVE ARRAY STRATEGY
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

def naive_update(arr: list, index: int, value: int) -> None:
    """Point update in O(1)."""
    arr[index] = value


def naive_range_sum(arr: list, l: int, r: int) -> int:
    """Range sum query in O(r - l + 1)."""
    total = 0
    for i in range(l, r + 1):
        total += arr[i]
    return total


def run_naive_benchmark(arr: list, operations: list) -> float:
    """Execute all Q operations on the raw array. Returns elapsed seconds."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for op in operations:
        if op[0] == 'update':
            naive_update(arr, op[1], op[2])
        else:  # 'query'
            naive_range_sum(arr, op[1], op[2])
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    return elapsed


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
#  2. SEGMENT TREE DATA STRUCTURE (from scratch)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

class SegmentTree:
    """
    Iterative-friendly recursive segment tree supporting:
      - build in Θ(N)
      - point update in O(log N)
      - range sum query in O(log N)
    Uses a 4*N sized array for the complete binary tree storage.
    """

    __slots__ = ('n', 'tree')

    def __init__(self, arr: list):
        self.n = len(arr)
        # Allocate 4*N to safely index a complete binary tree of N leaves
        self.tree = [0] * (4 * self.n)
        self._build(1, 0, self.n - 1, arr)

    # ---- Construction: T(N) = 2·T(N/2) + Θ(1)  →  Θ(N) ----
    def _build(self, node: int, lo: int, hi: int, arr: list) -> None:
        if lo == hi:
            self.tree[node] = arr[lo]
            return
        mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
        self._build(2 * node, lo, mid, arr)
        self._build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, arr)
        self.tree[node] = self.tree[2 * node] + self.tree[2 * node + 1]

    # ---- Point Update: traverses one root-to-leaf path, O(log N) ----
    def update(self, index: int, value: int) -> None:
        self._update(1, 0, self.n - 1, index, value)

    def _update(self, node: int, lo: int, hi: int, index: int, value: int) -> None:
        if lo == hi:
            self.tree[node] = value
            return
        mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
        if index <= mid:
            self._update(2 * node, lo, mid, index, value)
        else:
            self._update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, index, value)
        self.tree[node] = self.tree[2 * node] + self.tree[2 * node + 1]

    # ---- Range Sum Query: visits O(log N) nodes, O(log N) ----
    def query(self, l: int, r: int) -> int:
        return self._query(1, 0, self.n - 1, l, r)

    def _query(self, node: int, lo: int, hi: int, l: int, r: int) -> int:
        if r < lo or hi < l:
            return 0
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            return self.tree[node]
        mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
        return (self._query(2 * node, lo, mid, l, r) +
                self._query(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, l, r))


def run_segment_tree_benchmark(st: SegmentTree, operations: list) -> float:
    """Execute all Q operations on the segment tree. Returns elapsed seconds."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for op in operations:
        if op[0] == 'update':
            st.update(op[1], op[2])
        else:  # 'query'
            st.query(op[1], op[2])
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    return elapsed


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
#  3. SYNTHETIC DATASET & BENCHMARK DRIVER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────

def generate_workload(n: int, q: int, seed: int = 42):
    """
    Produce an initial array of N integers and Q intermixed
    point-update / range-sum operations.
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    arr = [rng.randint(-10**6, 10**6) for _ in range(n)]

    operations = []
    for _ in range(q):
        if rng.random() < 0.5:

            idx = rng.randint(0, n - 1)
            val = rng.randint(-10**6, 10**6)
            operations.append(('update', idx, val))
        else:
            # Range sum query [l, r] with 0 ≤ l ≤ r < N
            l = rng.randint(0, n - 1)
            r = rng.randint(l, n - 1)
            operations.append(('query', l, r))
    return arr, operations


def main():

    Q = 50_000

    print(f"    Updates  : {n_updates:,}")

    print(f"    Elapsed : {t_naive:.4f} s")

    # --- Benchmark: Segment Tree ---

Computational Musicology / DSP:
Synthesizes a C-Major triad (C4, E4, G4) with 2nd & 3rd harmonic overtones
using logarithmically decaying amplitudes, then applies an FFT to extract
and identify all frequency peaks in the resulting spectrum.

Dependencies: numpy, scipy

import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import rfft, rfftfreq
from scipy.signal import find_peaks

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. SIGNAL SYNTHESIS
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
SR = 44_100                          # sample rate (Hz)
DURATION = 1.0                       # duration (seconds)
N = int(SR * DURATION)               # total samples (44 100)
t = np.linspace(0.0, DURATION, N, endpoint=False)  # time axis

# C-Major triad fundamental frequencies (Hz)
FUNDAMENTALS = {
    "C4": 261.63,
    "E4": 329.63,
    "G4": 392.00,
}

def log_decay_amplitude(n: int) -> float:
    """
    Return the relative amplitude of the n-th harmonic (n >= 1)
    using a natural-logarithmic decay model, normalized so that
    the fundamental (n = 1) equals 1.0.

        A(n) = ln(2) / ln(n + 1)

    n=1 → 1.000
    n=2 → 0.631
    n=3 → 0.500
    """
    return np.log(2.0) / np.log(n + 1.0)

# Build the additive waveform
signal = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.float64)
for note_name, f0 in FUNDAMENTALS.items():
    for harmonic_order in range(1, 4):          # 1st, 2nd, 3rd partial
        amp = log_decay_amplitude(harmonic_order)
        f_partial = f0 * harmonic_order
        signal += amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * f_partial * t)

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2. FFT & SPECTRAL ANALYSIS

spectrum = rfft(signal)               # one-sided complex FFT
freqs    = rfftfreq(N, d=1.0 / SR)    # corresponding frequency bins (Hz)
magnitude = np.abs(spectrum)          # power spectrum (linear)

# Peak-picking parameters
height_threshold = np.max(magnitude) * 0.08   # 8 % of the global max
min_distance     = 10                        # minimum bins between peaks

peaks, _ = find_peaks(magnitude, height=height_threshold, distance=min_distance)
peak_freqs = freqs[peaks]
peak_mags  = magnitude[peaks]

# Sort ascending by frequency
order = np.argsort(peak_freqs)
peak_freqs = peak_freqs[order]
peak_mags  = peak_mags[order]

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# 3. PEAK IDENTIFICATION & REPORTING
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
def identify_peak(freq: float, fundamentals: dict, tol: float = 3.0) -> str:
    """Map a detected frequency to its nearest fundamental × harmonic."""
    best_label, best_err = "Unknown", float("inf")
    for note, f0 in fundamentals.items():
        for h in range(1, 4):
            expected = f0 * h
            err = abs(freq - expected)
            if err < best_err and err < tol:
                best_err = err
                best_label = f"{note} × {h}"
    return best_label

### I. Mathematical Mechanics of the Discrete Fourier Transform

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is the cornerstone of digital spectral analysis. For a finite-length signal $x[n]$ of $N$ samples, the DFT is defined as the complex-valued mapping

$$X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\; e^{-j2\pi kn/N}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, N{-}1,$$

which projects the time-domain sequence onto a basis of $N$ complex exponentials (the *roots of unity*). Each bin $X[k]$ encodes the amplitude and phase of the sinusoidal component at frequency $f_k = k\,f_s/N$, where $f_s$ is the sampling rate. The inverse transform $x[n] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_k X[k]\,e^{j2\pi kn/N}$ guarantees perfect reconstruction, a consequence of the orthogonality of the DFT basis vectors in $\mathbb{C}^N$. In practice, the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)—most commonly the Cooley–Tukey radix-2 algorithm—reduces the computational complexity from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ by exploiting the periodicity and symmetry of the twiddle factors $W_N^k = e^{-j2\pi k/N}$, enabling real-time spectral processing at audio sampling rates. The magnitude spectrum $|X[k]|$ (or its squared form, the periodogram) is what we interpret in the present script: each sinusoidal partial synthesized in the time domain appears as a sharp peak at its corresponding frequency bin, scaled by its amplitude and the windowing function (here, a rectangular window of length $N$).

### II. Psychoacoustics of Harmonic Spectra and Instrumental Timbre

The *timbre* of a musical sound is, in the Helmholtz–Rayleigh tradition, the perceptual attribute that distinguishes two tones of identical pitch, loudness, and duration. Psychophysically, timbre is encoded primarily by the relative amplitudes and temporal envelopes of the harmonic (and inharmonic) partials that constitute the signal. When a struck string or vibrating reed sets a resonant body into motion, the resulting waveform is a superposition of sinusoidal modes at integer multiples of the fundamental $f_0$: $x(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \sin(2\pi n f_0 t + \phi_n)$. The "brightness" or "darkness" of an instrument is governed by the rate at which $A_n$ decays with $n$; a piano's felt hammers produce a roughly $1/n$ roll-off, while a square wave sustains all odd harmonics at equal amplitude.
